title: Bitcoin's November Rout Revives 2022 Crypto Winter Comparisons
content:
Bitcoin is heading for one of its worst months in years, and the selling has spread through the crypto market.

## What happened

- Bitcoin fell to a **two-year low of roughly $55,600 around Nov. 21**, then rebounded to about **$60,000–$61,500**.
- Estimates of the month-to-date decline range from about **16% to 23%**, depending on the source and starting point.
- The price is now close to **50% below its October 2025 peak** of about $126,000.
- **Spot bitcoin ETFs saw heavy outflows.** Reported November totals range from about $2.9 billion to more than $5 billion, and BlackRock's IBIT reportedly posted its largest single-day outflow.
- More than **$2 billion of leveraged positions were liquidated** in a single 24-hour window during a mid-November weekend.

## Why now?

Analysts point to the same forces hitting tech stocks: expectations of another Fed rate hike, hot inflation data and a sell-off in AI and chip names. These have pushed investors away from speculative, high-volatility assets.

## The takeaway for investors

Crypto has fallen 50% or more from its highs several times before. If you hold it, size the position so that a drawdown like this doesn't derail your financial plan. A common guideline is to keep speculative assets to a small single-digit percentage of a portfolio.

*Sources: [TradingView / Crypto Briefing](https://www.tradingview.com/news/cryptobriefing:8a9200e0a094b:0-bitcoin-slides-as-much-as-23-in-november-2026-reviving-2022-bear-market-comparisons/), [KuCoin daily report, Nov. 27](https://www.kucoin.com/news/articles/crypto-daily-market-report-november-27-2026), [CEO Economy](https://ceoeconomy.com/article/crypto-week-in-review-nov-21-2026). Crypto data varies across exchanges and aggregators.*
summary: Bitcoin hit a two-year low near $55,600 before bouncing to around $61,000. Heavy outflows from spot bitcoin ETFs added to the pressure.
author: Staff Writer

title: S&P 500 Snaps Back After Longest Losing Streak Since 2020 as AI Trade Wobbles
content:
US stocks just had one of their most turbulent stretches in years, and the epicenter was the AI trade that has led the market for so long.

## What happened

- The **S&P 500 fell for seven consecutive sessions**, its longest losing streak since the pandemic crash of 2020.
- The **Nasdaq 100 dropped nearly 5% in early trading** at one point and briefly fell into **bear-market territory**, 20% below its recent high. Its swings were the largest since April 2025.
- On Wednesday, Nov. 25, the **Dow erased its losses and closed up about 0.3%**, while the S&P 500 slipped about 0.2% and the Nasdaq recovered part of its drop.
- Hot inflation data and expectations of another Fed rate hike added to pressure on high-valuation tech names.

## Why it matters

Because a handful of mega-cap tech companies make up a large share of the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100, a sell-off in those names hits index investors directly, even those who think they own "the whole market." Check how concentrated your fund really is on our [S&P 500 by weight](#/us-stocks/sp500) and [Nasdaq 100 by weight](#/us-stocks/nasdaq100) pages.

## The long view

Seven-day losing streaks feel dramatic but have happened many times in market history. Investors with a long horizon and a written allocation usually do best by rebalancing, not reacting. See [Rebalancing Your Portfolio](#/learn/rebalancing-your-portfolio).

*Sources: [Yahoo Finance live coverage, Nov. 25](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/live/stock-market-today-wednesday-november-25-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-pce-inflation-data-091428237.html), [BeInCrypto](https://beincrypto.com/tech-stocks-volatility-fed-rate-hike/).*
summary: Seven straight down days, a Nasdaq 100 dip into bear-market territory, then a partial recovery. Here's what drove a volatile week for US stocks.
author: Staff Writer

title: Mortgage Rates Ease to About 7.2% Heading Into Thanksgiving
content:
Homebuyers got a small break this week, though borrowing remains expensive by recent standards.

## The latest numbers

- The average **30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to about 7.21%** in Freddie Mac's survey released Wednesday, Nov. 25, down from roughly 7.28% the prior week.
- The Mortgage Bankers Association said in mid-November that borrowing costs had fallen almost 30 basis points from a nearly two-year high of about **7.5%** reached in October.
- A year ago, the 30-year rate was close to **6.2%**. Today's buyers pay about a full percentage point more.
- Daily trackers showed the average 30-year refinance rate near **7.0%**.

## What a 1% difference costs

On a 400,000 loan, a 30-year mortgage at 7.2% costs roughly 2,715 a month in principal and interest, against about 2,450 at 6.2%. That is around 265 more each month, or more than 95,000 over the life of the loan.

## What to do now

1. **Shop several lenders.** Quotes for the same borrower can differ meaningfully.
2. **Compare points against rate.** Paying points lowers the rate but only pays off if you keep the loan long enough.
3. **Don't stretch the budget** in the hope of refinancing later. Rates may not fall as quickly as expected, especially with the Fed expected to raise rates in December.

*Sources: [Fortune](https://fortune.com/article/current-mortgage-rates-11-23-2026/), [Bloomberg](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-11-11/us-mortgage-rates-fall-for-fourth-week-lifting-home-purchases), [RateZip](https://www.ratezip.com/news/mortgage-rates-today-2026-11-26). Figures vary by survey and lender.*
summary: Freddie Mac's weekly survey shows the 30-year fixed rate dipping to around 7.21%. That is modest relief for buyers, but still far above a year ago.
author: Staff Writer

title: Wall Street Still Expects a December Fed Hike, Even After Tech's Rough Month
content:
Investors who hoped falling tech stocks would soften the Federal Reserve's stance are being disappointed. Traders still see a rate hike as close to certain at the Fed's next meeting.

## What happened

- CME Group's FedWatch data put the probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the **Dec. 9 FOMC meeting** at roughly **98%** this week. Prediction market Polymarket showed somewhat lower odds, around 91%, down from about 98% in mid-November.
- Minutes from the October FOMC meeting showed a **strong consensus among officials in favor of raising rates in December**.
- The Fed's most recent move was a 25 bp hike in September, its first increase since 2023.
- Economist Claudia Sahm said the stock market would need to fall much further before it would change the Fed's course.

## Why it matters

A second hike would push borrowing costs higher just as growth worries build around the AI investment boom. Schwab noted that rate-hike expectations eased somewhat during the week, as some investors began to worry that a slowdown in AI spending could weigh on growth. For bond investors, higher policy rates usually mean pressure on longer-duration bonds. For savers, they mean better yields on cash.

## What to watch

The Dec. 9 decision and the Fed's updated projections, or "dot plot," for 2027. Any signal that this hike is the last one could matter as much as the hike itself.

*Sources: [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-fed-isnt-riding-to-the-rescue--wall-street-still-sees-a-december-rate-hike-after-techs-worst-week-since-2020-chart-of-the-day-110000273.html), [Schwab Weekly Trader's Outlook](https://www.schwab.com/learn/story/weekly-traders-outlook). Market-implied odds change daily.*
summary: Futures markets put the odds of a quarter-point Fed hike on Dec. 9 near 98%. A sharp sell-off in AI-linked stocks hasn't changed the central bank's hawkish message.
author: Staff Writer

title: House Committee Bill Would Write a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve Into Law
content:
Washington's crypto policy debate moved forward this week, even as bitcoin's price slid.

## What happened

- On Nov. 24, the **House Financial Services Committee** submitted the **American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026**.
- The bill would **codify a strategic bitcoin reserve** in law rather than leaving it to executive action.
- It proposes a **minimum 20-year holding period** for reserve bitcoin, aimed at preventing short-term selling.
- Separately, Switzerland's **BBIT spot bitcoin ETF** began trading, extending the range of regulated vehicles for crypto exposure in Europe.

## Why it matters

A legislated reserve would make the government a long-term holder and could reduce the risk of policy reversals. The bill still has to pass committee votes and both chambers of Congress, and its final form may differ substantially.

## What it doesn't change

Policy news rarely overrides market forces in the short run. The bill landed during bitcoin's steepest monthly decline in years. Investors should judge crypto on its role in their own portfolio, not on headlines.

*Sources: [Toobit market recap, Nov. 24](https://www.toobit.com/en-US/news/crypto-market-daily-recap-24-nov-2026), [KuCoin daily report](https://www.kucoin.com/news/articles/crypto-daily-market-report-november-27-2026). Bill details are as reported; consult the official text for specifics.*
summary: The American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026 would codify a US strategic bitcoin reserve and propose a minimum 20-year holding period.
author: Staff Writer

title: PCE Inflation Runs Hot at 3.8%, Keeping Pressure on the Fed
content:
The inflation measure the Federal Reserve watches most closely came in hotter than policymakers would like.

## By the numbers

| Measure | Year over year (October) |
|---|---|
| Headline PCE | **3.8%** |
| Core PCE (excluding food and energy) | **3.3%** |
| Fed target | 2.0% |

## What it means

The **personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index** tracks what households actually spend money on and is the Fed's official inflation benchmark. With both headline and core inflation well above target, the data strengthens the case for the rate hike markets expect on Dec. 9.

## Why it matters for your money

- **Cash and short-term bonds:** higher rates generally mean better yields on deposits and money-market funds.
- **Longer-term bonds:** rising rate expectations push their prices down. See [Why Bond Prices Fall When Interest Rates Rise](#/learn/interest-rates-and-bond-prices).
- **Stocks:** higher rates raise the discount rate on future profits, which weighs hardest on high-valuation growth stocks.

Track inflation, rates and other US data on our [US Economic Indicators](#/indicators/us) page.

*Sources: [Yahoo Finance](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/live/stock-market-today-wednesday-november-25-dow-sp-500-nasdaq-pce-inflation-data-091428237.html), [Yahoo Finance Chart of the Day](https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/article/the-fed-isnt-riding-to-the-rescue--wall-street-still-sees-a-december-rate-hike-after-techs-worst-week-since-2020-chart-of-the-day-110000273.html).*
summary: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge rose 3.8% year over year in October, with core PCE at 3.3%, well above the central bank's 2% target.

title: Warren Buffett: Handing Over the Keys, Giving Away the Company
content:
Warren Buffett just handed the keys to Greg Abel — and started giving the company away.

- Berkshire's Q3 2026 13F (filed Nov 16): $304B across 30 holdings.
- Trimmed Bank of America by 5.7% (-0.52% portfolio impact).
- New position: Bending Spoons SpA, 20.69M shares.
- Personally converted 6,150 Class A shares into 9.225M Class B shares — a $5.5B gift to four family foundations.

Succession isn't a future event anymore — it's already running the portfolio.
summary: Berkshire's Q3 13F trimmed Bank of America and added a new stake in Bending Spoons, while Buffett personally gifted $5.5B in shares to his family foundations.
author: Staff Writer

title: TSMC's October Revenue Grew 59.7% — Before the Stock Even Noticed
content:
## What happened

- TSMC reported October 2026 net revenue of approximately NT$586.89 billion, up 14.7% month-over-month and up 59.7% year-over-year, in a Form 6-K filed with the SEC on Nov 10.
- January-October 2026 cumulative revenue totaled NT$4,485.62 billion, up 43.3% versus the same period in 2025.
- This filing landed before the Nvidia CEO-reinstatement rally that later sent TSM shares up 14.08% on Nov 23 — its best single-day gain since October 2008.
- The October numbers are a reminder that the rally had real demand underneath it, not just sentiment: TSMC manufactures most of Nvidia's advanced AI accelerator chips.

## Why it matters

A 14% single-day pop driven by a CEO headline is a sentiment move. A 59.7% year-over-year revenue jump filed with the SEC two weeks earlier is a fundamentals move. Both are true at once here, and it's worth being able to tell them apart when the next headline hits.
summary: Taiwan Semiconductor's SEC filing shows October 2026 revenue up 59.7% year-over-year and ten-month cumulative revenue up 43.3% — the demand story underneath this week's historic rally.
author: Staff Writer

title: TSMC (TSM): Why Nvidia's Drama Is TSMC's Drama Too
content:
If you want proof that TSMC's stock is a direct read-through on Nvidia, November 2026 is the textbook case.

## A month that tracked Nvidia almost tick for tick

- **Nov 12:** TSM fell 1.9% to $405.49 on the news of Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia.
- **Nov 17:** TSM dropped 3.7% to $359.69 after media tied the move to a new US rule tightening checks on chip foundries.
- **Nov 20:** TSM fell another 9.5% to $318.71.
- **Nov 23:** The moment Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO, TSM rocketed **14.1%** to close at $363.60 — its best day in years, directly tied to its role as Nvidia's exclusive manufacturing partner.
- Earlier in the month, TSM had jumped 6.3% on an unconfirmed report that it's drawing up plans to build stacked DRAM for Nvidia — nothing signed yet, but the market treated it as a credible signal.

## The bigger picture

Even after the big bounce, TSM still sits roughly **25% below its 52-week high**, despite outperforming the Nasdaq by 7.6 percentage points over the stretch. That gap is the clearest sign of how much "Nvidia risk" is currently priced into TSMC shares — for better and for worse.

## Why it matters

TSMC's fundamentals (foundry capacity, node leadership, customer backlog) move slowly. Its stock price, this month, moved entirely on headlines about one customer's leadership and export-control rules. That's the concentration risk every TSMC investor is implicitly taking on.
summary: TSM surged 14.1% the moment Jensen Huang was reinstated as Nvidia's CEO — a reminder of just how tightly TSMC's fortunes are tied to its biggest customer.
author: Staff Writer

title: Ray Dalio: Cautious on Stocks and Bonds, Still Anchored in Index Funds
content:
Ray Dalio doesn't love stocks or bonds right now — but he's still holding plenty of both.

- Bridgewater's $23B stock portfolio still keeps 16% in SPY and IVV, even after cutting both.
- Dalio's long-run expected return for the S&P 500: just 4.7% a year — below his ~5% estimate for long bonds.
- His stated concern: stretched valuations, high P/E multiples, tight credit spreads.
- He's hinting at a preference for non-US equities, bonds, and currencies as a dollar-decline hedge.
- Portfolio value: ~$22.99B as of Nov 22, 2026, still anchored by broad index funds.

Caution at the macro level, index-fund dependence at the portfolio level — a very Dalio combination.
summary: Dalio pegs long-run S&P 500 returns at just 4.7% a year amid stretched valuations — yet Bridgewater still keeps 16% of its $23B stock book in SPY and IVV.
author: Staff Writer

title: Nvidia (NVDA): The SEC Probe Didn't Go Away When Huang Came Back
content:
## What happened

- Reuters reported Nov 19 that the SEC is probing Nvidia's accounting practices; California Attorney General Rob Bonta served the company with an investigative subpoena the same week.
- That overhang helped drive NVDA down 14.0% to $125.53 on Nov 20 — a fresh 52-week low — even before the CEO-resignation drama peaked days later.
- Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO on Nov 22-23 triggered a 31%+ single-day rally, but CNBC's Nov 24 follow-up ("Nvidia brought Jensen Huang back. But the investigations aren't over") makes clear the SEC probe, DOJ attention, and congressional scrutiny are all still active.
- None of the legal questions have been resolved — only the leadership question has.

## Why it matters

A reinstated CEO fixed the governance headline, not the accounting one. Investors cheering the rally should keep an eye on how the SEC and California AG proceedings develop — that's the overhang that doesn't go away with a board vote.
summary: Even after Jensen Huang's reinstatement sent NVDA up 31%, an SEC accounting probe and a California AG subpoena are still active — CNBC reports DOJ and congressional scrutiny remain in play too.
author: Staff Writer

title: Nvidia's Q3: Revenue Up 103%, But Nobody Was Talking About It
content:
## What happened

- Nvidia's fiscal quarterly report, released Nov 17, showed revenue up 103% year-over-year to $115.8 billion.
- Net income rose 105% year-over-year to $65.3 billion.
- Within days, the board-level drama around Jensen Huang's resignation and reinstatement took over the headlines, and the earnings beat barely registered in the broader coverage.
- The fundamentals behind the AI buildout — chip demand, data-center spend — didn't change because of a leadership story.

## Why it matters

It's worth separating the two narratives: the governance and legal overhang is real and unresolved, but the underlying demand numbers from this report were genuinely strong. Investors evaluating Nvidia should weigh both threads independently rather than letting one drown out the other.
summary: Nvidia's Nov 17 quarterly report showed revenue up 103% year-over-year to $115.8B and net income up 105% to $65.3B — numbers that got buried under the CEO-resignation news that broke days later.
author: Staff Writer

title: Nvidia (NVDA): Jensen Huang Is Back, and the Market Noticed
content:
Nvidia just had one of the wildest two-week stretches in its history — and it ended with the stock up over 30% in a day.

## What happened

- **Nov 20:** NVDA fell 14.0% to $125.53 after a Reuters report that the SEC is probing the company's accounting. The stock had already slumped more than 40% over the prior month.
- **Nov 23:** Nvidia's board unanimously voted to reinstate **Jensen Huang** as President and CEO, effective immediately — less than two weeks after he had resigned. NVDA closed at $165.05, up **31.5%** on the day.
- The rally recovered roughly **$952B** of the **$1.16T** in market value Nvidia had lost, and it dragged the broader AI trade back up with it — all three major U.S. indexes had just closed Friday in a correction.
- **Melius Research** upgraded NVDA to Buy with a $220 price target; **Bernstein** moved to Outperform with a $200 target.
- A sobering note: the stock gave back more than 5% the very next trading session, a reminder that this move was driven by a leadership decision, not a change in underlying fundamentals.

## Why it matters

Nvidia isn't just a chipmaker right now — it's the bellwether for the entire AI trade. When its CEO situation wobbles, it drags Big Tech with it; when it stabilizes, the relief rally is market-wide. Keep watching the SEC accounting probe — that overhang didn't disappear just because Huang came back.
summary: NVDA stock jumped 31.5% in a single session after the board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, just two weeks after an SEC-probe-driven selloff wiped over $1T off its market cap.
author: Staff Writer

title: Michael Burry: Unwinding the Nvidia Bet, Doubling Down on Value
content:
Michael Burry just un-shorted Nvidia — sort of.

- Sold 75% of his NVDA put options after the SEC-probe-driven selloff.
- Bought long-dated, out-of-the-money NVDA calls as a hedge, keeping some short-dated puts.
- Closed out ALL his semiconductor ETF (SMH) put positions, citing rich option premiums.
- Trimmed Nasdaq-100 put exposure by half; locked in gains on Zoetis calls.
- Biggest longs: MercadoLibre (stake up 20%) and Temple & Webster, each over 10% of the book.

He calls NVDA "a heck of a trade" — but his real conviction is still in beaten-down value, not AI.
summary: Burry sold 75% of his NVDA puts and closed out his semiconductor ETF shorts entirely, while quietly increasing his biggest long positions in MercadoLibre and Temple & Webster.

title: Intel (INTC): Shareholder Lawsuit Lands Right as Foundry Losses Mount
content:
## What happened

- A shareholder class action covering investors who bought INTC shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026 names CEO Lip-Bu Tan and CFO David Zinsner as defendants, alleging Intel failed to promptly disclose how falling PC sales and inventory buildup would hit revenue.
- INTC fell 7.0% to $55.47 on Nov 16, a drop tied partly to the suit and partly to a sector-wide AI-chip selloff ahead of Nvidia's earnings.
- Separately, Intel's foundry business posted a $1.85 billion operating loss last quarter, and the company has said it likely won't generate positive free cash flow next year.
- The stock has since been volatile with the broader chip sector — up over 13% on Nov 23 amid the Huang-reinstatement rally, then down 8.1% on Nov 24 as that rally cooled.

## Why it matters

Intel's foundry turnaround was always going to be a multi-year, cash-intensive bet — this is the market pricing in that it's taking longer and costing more than hoped, layered on top of a fresh legal question about what management knew and when. Both threads are separate from the sector-wide chip volatility and worth tracking on their own.
summary: A new class action accuses Intel's CEO and CFO of sitting on bad news about falling PC sales and inventory buildup, while the foundry business posted a $1.85B quarterly operating loss.
author: Staff Writer

title: Intel (INTC): Volatile Month, but the 18A Bet Is Starting to Pay Off
content:
Intel's November has been a story of two very different narratives fighting for control of the stock.

## The rough patch

- **Nov 16:** INTC fell 7.0% to $55.47 after a shareholder class action named CEO **Lip-Bu Tan** and CFO **David Zinsner** as defendants, alleging Intel didn't promptly disclose how falling PC sales and an inventory buildup would hit revenue. The suit covers investors who bought shares between July 23 and October 29, 2026.
- The same week, a filing showed **Nvidia cut its stake in Intel by 25%**.

## The turnaround signal

- **Nov 9:** INTC rose 5.5% to $59.37 as chip stocks broadly rebounded.
- **Nov 18:** Intel signed its **first external customer for advanced 18A chips** — a genuine proof point for the foundry turnaround strategy — and announced an expanded Microsoft Azure collaboration the same day.
- Despite the lawsuit and the pullback, INTC is still **up 48% year-to-date**, powered by surging server demand and real progress on the manufacturing side. Some analysts now see a path back toward **$85** on the strength of the 18A win.

## Why it matters

The lawsuit is a real overhang, but it's a backward-looking dispute about disclosure timing. The 18A customer win is forward-looking and strikes at the core question investors have had about Intel for years: can its foundry business actually compete? One external customer isn't proof, but it's the first real data point.
summary: Intel swung between a shareholder lawsuit and a landmark first external customer for its 18A chips — and is still up 48% year-to-date despite a brutal month.

title: Bill Ackman: Calling the Market a Casino, Then Betting $2B Anyway
content:
Bill Ackman just called the market a "casino" — then put $2B into two new stocks.

author: Staff Writer

title: Apple's Record Year Came With a Margin Warning
content:
## What happened

- On its Nov 2 earnings call, Apple reported fiscal Q4 2026 revenue of $114.5 billion and net income of $30.7 billion, both beating estimates.
- That capped a record fiscal year: $478.8 billion in annual revenue, up 15% year-over-year.
- AAPL still fell 1.9% to $331.90 on Nov 3 after management guided December-quarter gross margin to 45-46%, below what analysts had modeled.
- The stock has since recovered well beyond that level, closing above $350 for the first time on Nov 9 and setting a fresh record close of $356.27 on Nov 13, pushing Apple's market cap past $5 trillion.

## Why it matters

The margin guidance is the detail that matters more than the headline beat: it's management's own read on near-term cost pressure, and it's the number analysts will be checking against next quarter regardless of where the stock price has since drifted.
summary: Apple closed fiscal 2026 with $478.8B in annual revenue, up 15%, but the stock dipped after management guided December-quarter gross margin to 45-46%, below analyst estimates.
author: Staff Writer

title: Apple's iCloud, App Store, and Apple Pay Went Down
content:
## What happened

- Apple's iCloud, App Store, and Apple Pay services went down on Nov 17 following an internal software update.
- The outage affected users broadly across these core services before being resolved.
- It landed in the same week as Apple's run toward a $5 trillion market cap, a reminder that scale doesn't eliminate operational risk.

## Why it matters

Outages like this rarely move the stock on their own, but they're worth tracking as a pattern — services revenue (iCloud, App Store, Apple Pay) is an increasingly important slice of Apple's business, and reliability there matters to the thesis.
summary: A software update triggered an outage across iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Pay on Nov 17 — a reminder that even a $5T company carries operational risk.
author: Staff Writer

title: Apple (AAPL): A $5 Trillion Milestone, With a Margin Asterisk
content:
Apple just hit a number that sounds almost unreal: a $5 trillion market capitalization, backed by its first-ever close above $350 a share.

## The milestone

- Apple's 12-month return through Nov 12 was **29.4%**, more than double the S&P 500's 12.2% over the same stretch.
- **Nov 9:** AAPL rose 2.43% to a record close of $350.69.
- **Nov 4:** AAPL rose 5.3% to $349.51 as Big Tech rallied broadly after the midterm elections.
- The stock now trades **above** the average analyst price target of $340.77 (from 45 analysts), who collectively rate it a consensus Buy.

## The asterisk

- **Nov 2 earnings:** Revenue hit **$478.8B, up 15%** year over year — a strong headline number.
- But guidance spooked some investors: management guided December-quarter gross margin to **45–46%**, down from 47.9% in the September quarter. AAPL fell 1.9% to $331.90 on Nov 3 as a result.
- Executives pointed to two specific causes: **rising memory costs** and the ramp-up spend on the **Siri AI overhaul**.

## Why it matters

The $5T headline is the story everyone will share. The margin guidance is the story worth actually tracking — Apple is explicitly trading some near-term profitability for an AI bet on Siri, at the same time memory input costs are rising industry-wide (the same dynamic hitting plenty of other hardware makers right now). Revenue growth is real; the margin trade-off is the thing to watch into next quarter's print.
summary: Apple closed above $350 for the first time and crossed the $5 trillion market cap mark — but its own guidance flagged rising memory costs and Siri AI spend squeezing margins.
author: Staff Writer

title: AMD's Whiplash Week: Short-Seller Report, China Ties, and a $2.5B Anthropic Bet
content:
## What happened

- AMD fell 13.25% to $424.39 on Nov 20 after a short-seller report on its China ties deepened a sector-wide AI-chip selloff, then fell another 8.9% on Nov 24 as chips gave back gains from the Nvidia-reinstatement rally.
- On the positive side, AMD is investing $2.5 billion in Anthropic, part of an up-to-$5-billion chip-delivery-linked commitment announced around Nov 10.
- AMD posted record Q3 revenue of $13.4 billion on Nov 3, with Q4 guidance of roughly $17 billion.
- Not on the core watchlist, but AMD is directly entangled in this month's chip-sector story — the Nvidia CEO saga, the new export-control rule, and the AI capex buildout all move its stock too.

## Why it matters

AMD is a useful cross-check on the Nvidia/TSMC narrative: when the sector-wide story is sentiment-driven (CEO drama, export rules), AMD swings with it; when it's about AMD's own execution (the Anthropic deal, the Q3 beat), the stock has separate, company-specific reasons to move. Worth distinguishing which is which before reacting to any single day's move.
summary: AMD fell 13.25% on a short-seller report about its China exposure, then gave back more gains on Nov 24 — even as it deepens a $2.5B investment tied to Anthropic and posts record Q3 revenue.

title: Amazon's Rough Week: FAA Investigates a Drone Crash, a Satellite Launch Fails
content:
## What happened

- The FAA is investigating an Amazon delivery drone crash in Michigan near Detroit, confirmed as of Nov 24.
- Earlier in the month, a failed launch of an Amazon "Leo" satellite was cited alongside a new US AI chip export restriction rule as factors behind AMZN falling 3.34% to $257.75 on Nov 16.
- Neither incident is financially material on its own, but together they represent two different Amazon frontier bets — autonomous delivery and satellite internet — hitting operational snags in the same stretch.

## Why it matters

Amazon is running several capital-intensive moonshots at once (drones, Kuiper satellites, AI infrastructure). Isolated setbacks are normal at this stage, but it's worth tracking whether they cluster into a pattern or stay one-off.
summary: The FAA is investigating an Amazon delivery drone crash near Detroit, compounding a week that also saw a failed Leo satellite launch and a 3.3% stock drop.

title: Amazon Buys Decart's AI Chip-Software Team
content:
## What happened

- Amazon announced on Nov 23 that it is acquiring AI startup Decart's chip-software technology and hiring its founding team.
- The deal is squarely about compute infrastructure — software that sits closer to the chip layer — rather than a consumer-facing AI product.
- It comes in the same month Amazon disclosed heavier AWS capital spending tied to its broader AI buildout, including its Anthropic relationship.

## Why it matters

Amazon keeps making small, infrastructure-layer acquisitions rather than one big headline deal — a pattern worth watching alongside its AWS capex trajectory, since this is where the AI margin story will actually get decided.
summary: Amazon announced Nov 23 it's acquiring AI startup Decart's chip-software technology and hiring its founders — another quiet move to control more of its own AI compute stack.

title: Amazon (AMZN): A Rough November, a Massive AI Bet Behind It
content:
Amazon's stock chart in November tells a story of short-term stumbles layered on top of an enormous, deliberate AI bet.

## The stumbles

- **Nov 5:** AMZN fell 2.2% as a broad tech selloff erased early gains from its new Uber Eats partnership for Prime members.
- **Nov 11:** AMZN fell 1.7% on Anthropic's amended IPO filing — notable because Amazon holds a **14.6% stake** in Anthropic.
- **Nov 16:** AMZN fell 3.3% after the loss of 40 **Amazon Leo** satellites in a failed rocket launch, compounded by a new US rule tightening access to advanced AI chips.
- **Nov 19:** AMZN fell 3.9% following Anthropic's actual Nasdaq debut — the stake that was supposed to be a tailwind instead coincided with a down day for AMZN itself.

## The bigger bet underneath

- CEO **Andy Jassy** is pushing roughly **$220 billion** in 2026 capex, overwhelmingly directed at data centers, servers, and networking to support AWS and Amazon Bedrock.
- Despite the choppy month, analysts have been raising targets: **UBS to $352**, **Freedom Broker from $255 to $330**, and **Oppenheimer to $310** after the Anthropic IPO.
- Amazon is also reportedly eyeing a **$7.5B AI startup deal** as competition with Nvidia's ecosystem heats up.

## Why it matters

None of November's drops were about Amazon's core retail or cloud business underperforming — they were about AI-adjacent headline risk (a satellite failure, chip export rules, a related company's IPO). Meanwhile, the capex number and the analyst target hikes suggest the people who cover this stock closely aren't rattled by the daily noise. Worth separating the headline-driven dips from the underlying thesis.
summary: AMZN slid repeatedly through November on satellite setbacks and Anthropic IPO jitters — even as Andy Jassy leans into a $220B AI capex plan and analysts keep raising targets.

title: Washington Tightens AI Chip Export Rules — and NVDA, TSM, AMD All Felt It
content:
## What happened

- On Nov 16, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security issued a rule requiring licenses for AI chip or server exports to data centers anywhere in the world if the compute could reach China or other restricted countries, and added new licensing requirements for Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil.
- Reporting explicitly linked the tightened rule to the Nvidia espionage scandal that preceded Jensen Huang's temporary resignation.
- AMD fell roughly 4-5% on Nov 16 on the news; Nvidia separately warned chip buyers of legal risk tied to China AI access.
- Separately, it was reported on Nov 19 that the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China over the prior six months — a reminder the policy picture is not a simple one-way clampdown.

## Why it matters

Export-control policy is now a first-order risk factor for the entire AI chip supply chain — Nvidia, TSMC, and AMD all move on these headlines independent of their own earnings. Worth tracking as its own story line, separate from any single company's quarter.
summary: A new Commerce Department rule closes a 'remote access' loophole for AI chip exports to China and adds licensing hurdles for Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, and Brazil — reporting ties it explicitly to the Nvidia espionage scandal.

title: How to Read a Drawdown Chart (and Why It Matters)
content:
Most performance summaries lead with the happy numbers: total return, CAGR, ending balance. A drawdown chart tells the other half of the story — how far the investment fell from its previous peak, and how long it took to climb back.

## What a drawdown actually measures

A drawdown is the percentage decline from a previous all-time high to a subsequent low, before a new high is reached. If a portfolio grows to $100,000, then falls to $70,000 before eventually recovering, that's a 30% drawdown — regardless of what the portfolio does afterward.

Three numbers describe every drawdown:

- **Depth** — how far it fell (30% in the example above).
- **Length** — how many days or months it took to go from peak to trough.
- **Recovery time** — how long after the trough it took to reach a new all-time high.

## Why depth alone isn't the full picture

A 20% drawdown that recovers in three months is a very different experience than a 20% drawdown that takes three years to recover. The first is a rough quarter. The second means someone checking their portfolio regularly spent three years watching a number that never got back to where it started — even though the eventual long-term return might look fine on a 20-year chart.

This is why "worst drawdown" and "longest drawdown" are both worth checking, not just one. A strategy's *maximum* drawdown tells you the worst single hit; the recovery length tells you how long you'd need to stay disciplined through it.

## Why this matters more than average volatility

Standard deviation (a common volatility measure) describes how much an investment typically wiggles around its average. Drawdown describes the single worst real experience an investor actually lived through. For most people, it's the drawdown — not the average volatility — that determines whether they can stick with a plan.

This is also why drawdown analysis is a useful gut-check before committing to an asset. It's easy to look at a 10-year average return and feel confident. It's harder to look at "this investment lost 45% of its value and took two years to recover" and honestly ask whether you'd have held on.

## Using drawdown data well

- Look at the **worst drawdown**, not just the average return, before deciding how much of a portfolio to allocate to a volatile asset.
- Check the **recovery time**, not just the depth — a fast recovery is a very different risk than a slow one.
- Compare drawdowns **across assets** for the same historical period. Two investments can have similar long-term CAGR while one asked investors to tolerate a far rougher ride to get there.

A backtest that only reports the ending balance is hiding the part of the story that determines whether a real person would have actually stayed invested long enough to reach it.
summary: A drawdown chart shows the worst-case emotional experience of holding an investment, not just its long-term average. Here's how to interpret one.
author: Staff Writer

title: The Case for Dollar-Cost Averaging in Volatile Markets
content:
Volatile markets create a very specific kind of pressure: prices are moving so much that it feels like there must be a "right" moment to invest, if only you could identify it. Dollar-cost averaging (DCA) is the strategy of ignoring that pressure entirely — investing a fixed amount on a fixed schedule, regardless of what price is doing that day.

## Why timing is harder than it looks

To beat DCA through timing, you don't just need to correctly identify that a downturn is happening — you need to correctly identify *when it ends*, so you can deploy your cash before the recovery. Missing that window, even by a few weeks, can erase the advantage of having waited in the first place.

Historically, some of the market's strongest days have clustered right after its worst ones. An investor who sits in cash waiting for "the bottom" risks being out of the market precisely when it snaps back — and there's no reliable signal that tells you the bottom has passed until well after the fact.

## What DCA actually does mechanically

When you invest a fixed dollar amount on a schedule, you automatically buy more shares when prices are low and fewer shares when prices are high. You don't need to predict anything — the math does the work. Over a volatile period, this tends to produce a lower average cost per share than trying to time lump-sum entries.

This doesn't mean DCA always beats a lump sum investment — in a steadily rising market, investing everything upfront usually wins, simply because more money spends more time invested. DCA's real value shows up specifically during volatile or declining stretches, which is exactly when the temptation to stop contributing is strongest.

## The behavioral case is as strong as the math

Arguably the bigger benefit of DCA isn't mathematical — it's psychological. A fixed schedule removes the decision point where fear or excitement can take over. There's no daily choice to make about whether "now" is a good time to invest, which means there's no daily opportunity to talk yourself out of it.

This matters because the biggest risk to most long-term investment plans isn't picking the wrong asset — it's abandoning a reasonable plan at the worst possible moment, usually during a downturn, out of fear.

## Putting it into practice

A DCA plan doesn't need to be complicated:

1. Decide a contribution amount you can sustain even in a bad month, not just a good one.
2. Automate it on a fixed schedule — monthly is common — so it doesn't depend on remembering or feeling motivated.
3. Leave it running through both up and down periods. The strategy's benefit specifically comes from not stopping when things look scary.

Backtesting a contribution schedule against a genuinely volatile historical period — rather than just a smooth bull run — is the clearest way to see this effect for yourself.
summary: When prices are swinging wildly, the instinct is to wait for a better entry point. Here's why a fixed, boring contribution schedule usually wins anyway.
author: Staff Writer

title: SPY vs. QQQ vs. MSCI World: Choosing the Right Index Fund
content:
"Just buy an index fund" is common advice — but which index? SPY, QQQ, and MSCI World all get recommended as simple, diversified core holdings, yet they're meaningfully different products.

## SPY: the S&P 500

SPY tracks the S&P 500, roughly the 500 largest publicly traded U.S. companies, weighted by market capitalization. It's broad within the U.S. market — spanning technology, healthcare, financials, energy, and more — but it is entirely U.S.-based.

Because it's weighted by market cap, SPY's performance is still meaningfully influenced by its largest holdings, which in recent years have skewed heavily toward a handful of large technology companies. It's diversified across sectors, but concentrated at the top.

## QQQ: the Nasdaq 100

QQQ tracks the 100 largest non-financial companies listed on the Nasdaq. In practice, this means a much heavier tilt toward technology and growth companies than SPY. QQQ has historically delivered strong returns during tech-driven bull markets, but that same concentration means it can fall harder during tech-sector downturns.

QQQ is not really a "total market" fund — it's a growth-and-tech-tilted fund that happens to be popular enough to be treated like one. Worth knowing before assuming it behaves like a generic index.

## MSCI World: true global diversification

MSCI World (tracked by ETFs like URTH) holds large and mid-cap companies across roughly two dozen developed markets, including the U.S., Japan, the U.K., and much of Europe. This gives it geographic diversification that SPY and QQQ don't have — if the U.S. market underperforms for a stretch, other developed markets in the index may not.

The tradeoff is that MSCI World is still heavily weighted toward the U.S. (U.S. companies make up a large share of global market capitalization), so the diversification benefit is real but partial, not a complete hedge against U.S.-specific downturns.

## How to think about the choice

- **Want simple, broad U.S. exposure?** SPY is the standard choice, and its long history makes it easy to backtest against decades of data.
- **Want to lean into growth and technology, understanding the extra volatility that comes with it?** QQQ fits, but should be sized as a satellite holding for many investors rather than a sole core position.
- **Want geographic diversification beyond the U.S.?** MSCI World spreads exposure across developed markets, at the cost of somewhat lower historical returns compared to SPY over the last decade.

None of these is objectively "best" — they answer different questions about how much concentration and geography you're comfortable with. Running the same contribution schedule through a backtest against each one is a fast way to see how differently they've actually behaved.
summary: All three are popular 'just buy the index' choices, but they hold very different companies and carry different risk profiles. Here's how they actually differ.
author: Staff Writer

title: Reading Economic Indicators Like a Pro
content:
Economic indicators can feel like noise: a constant stream of releases, revisions, and headlines reacting to each one. For a long-term investor, most of that noise is safely ignorable. A handful of indicators, though, are worth understanding because they describe the environment your investments are growing in.

## Inflation (CPI)

The Consumer Price Index measures how fast prices for goods and services are rising. It matters to investors for a simple reason: your portfolio isn't just trying to grow in dollar terms, it's trying to grow in *purchasing power* terms. A 7% annual return during a year of 6% inflation is a very different outcome than a 7% return during a year of 1% inflation.

Central banks also watch CPI closely, because sustained high inflation typically triggers interest rate hikes — which brings us to the next indicator.

## Interest rates

Interest rates set by central banks ripple through nearly every asset class. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, which tends to cool off economic growth and can pressure stock valuations (future company earnings are worth less in today's dollars when discounted at a higher rate). Lower rates tend to do the opposite.

For a long-term index investor, interest rate cycles are less about timing trades and more about understanding *why* markets are moving the way they are in a given period — context that makes volatility easier to sit through.

## GDP growth

Gross Domestic Product measures the total economic output of a country. Slowing GDP growth (or two consecutive quarters of contraction, commonly used as a rule of thumb for recession) tends to coincide with weaker corporate earnings, which eventually shows up in stock prices.

GDP is a backward-looking, slow-moving number — it won't help you predict next week's market move. Its value is in understanding the broader economic cycle a market is in.

## Unemployment

Unemployment is a lagging indicator: it tends to move *after* the economy has already turned, not before. Rising unemployment usually confirms a slowdown that other indicators (like GDP or manufacturing activity) already hinted at. Falling unemployment in a strong economy supports consumer spending, which supports corporate revenue.

## The takeaway

No single indicator predicts market direction reliably — if it did, everyone would trade on it and the edge would disappear. What these numbers are good for is building context: understanding *why* a backtest period included a rough stretch, or why a particular country's market moved differently than another's. Use them to understand the environment, not to time your next contribution.
summary: GDP, CPI, unemployment — the indicators dashboard surfaces dozens of numbers. Here's how to tell which ones actually matter for a long-term investor.
author: Staff Writer

title: Understanding CAGR, Sharpe, and Sortino Ratios
content:
If you've run a backtest, you've seen these three metrics sitting next to the ending balance. They look similar — all just numbers describing performance — but each answers a different question.

## CAGR: how fast did it actually grow?

CAGR (Compound Annual Growth Rate) answers: "If this investment grew at a steady, constant rate every year, what would that rate be?" It smooths out the bumpy year-to-year returns into a single, comparable number.

CAGR is useful precisely because raw total return is hard to compare across different time periods. A 50% total return sounds great — until you learn it happened over 15 years, which is a very different result than 50% over 2 years. CAGR normalizes for time, which is why it's the standard way to compare investments.

What CAGR *doesn't* tell you is anything about the ride along the way. Two investments can post the same CAGR while one moved in a straight line and the other swung wildly.

## Sharpe ratio: was the return worth the volatility?

The Sharpe ratio asks a sharper question: "How much return did you earn *per unit of risk taken*?" It's calculated by taking the return above a risk-free rate and dividing by the standard deviation of returns (volatility).

A higher Sharpe ratio means you got more return for the bumps you endured. A low Sharpe ratio can mean one of two things: either the returns were mediocre, or the ride was so volatile that the returns don't really compensate for the stress of holding through it.

This is why comparing two strategies by CAGR alone can be misleading. A strategy with a slightly lower CAGR but a much higher Sharpe ratio might be the better real-world choice, because it delivers similar results with far less turbulence.

## Sortino ratio: what about just the downside?

The Sortino ratio is a variation on the Sharpe ratio with one key difference: it only penalizes *downside* volatility, not volatility in general.

This distinction matters because standard deviation (used in the Sharpe ratio) treats a sudden 10% jump upward the same as a sudden 10% drop — both count as "volatility." Most investors, however, don't actually mind upside swings; what they care about is downside risk. The Sortino ratio isolates that, which is why it's often considered a more intuitive risk-adjusted measure for long-term investors.

## Putting it together

None of these numbers should be read in isolation:

- **CAGR** tells you the growth rate.
- **Sharpe ratio** tells you whether that growth came with excessive volatility, good and bad.
- **Sortino ratio** tells you specifically about the downside risk you were exposed to.

A strategy with a high CAGR, a poor Sharpe ratio, and an even worse Sortino ratio is one that likely delivered its gains through a genuinely rough ride — worth knowing before committing real savings to it.
summary: Three numbers show up in almost every portfolio report. Here's what each one actually measures, and why looking at return alone can be misleading.
author: Staff Writer

title: Why Backtesting Beats Guesswork
content:
Most investing decisions get made on vibes. Someone reads a headline, feels confident (or scared), and adjusts their portfolio accordingly. Backtesting is the antidote to that: it replaces "I think this would work" with "here is what actually happened when someone did this."

## What backtesting actually tells you

A backtest takes a strategy — an asset, a starting amount, a contribution schedule — and replays it against real historical prices. Instead of imagining how an investment might have grown, you get the actual numbers: the ending balance, the annualized return, the worst drawdown along the way, and how long recovery took.

This matters because intuition is bad at two things in particular:

- **Estimating compounding.** Most people underestimate how much a modest monthly contribution grows over 10+ years, because linear thinking doesn't capture exponential growth.
- **Estimating pain.** It's easy to say "I can handle a 30% drop" in the abstract. It's different to see that a real drawdown lasted 18 months and erased three years of contributions before recovering.

## Backtesting isn't a crystal ball

It's important to be precise about what a backtest is *not*. A backtest tells you how a strategy performed over one specific historical path. It does not guarantee that path will repeat. Markets that delivered a 10% CAGR over the last decade won't necessarily deliver 10% over the next one.

What a backtest is good for is **stress-testing assumptions**. If your plan only works when everything goes well, a backtest across a period that includes a real crash (2008, 2020, 2022) will expose that quickly. If your plan survives those periods and still ends up ahead, that's meaningfully more evidence than a gut feeling.

## How to use a backtest well

1. **Pick a long enough window.** A 2-year backtest mostly tells you about 2 years of luck. Look at 10+ year windows when you can, and check multiple starting points.
2. **Include contributions, not just a lump sum.** Most real investors add money over time. A backtest that only models a single upfront deposit misses how dollar-cost averaging changes the outcome.
3. **Look past the ending balance.** Two strategies can end at the same balance with very different journeys — one with a smooth ride, one with a stomach-churning 40% drawdown in the middle. Check the volatility and max drawdown figures, not just the final number.
4. **Compare against a simple baseline.** Before trusting a complex strategy, check how a plain index fund would have done over the same period. Often, it's a tough benchmark to beat.

Backtesting won't tell you the future. But it will replace guesses with evidence, and that alone tends to produce better decisions.
summary: Before you commit real money to a strategy, backtesting lets you see how it would have actually performed through real bull markets, crashes, and everything in between.
